title: Live dashboard — real application, synthetic data
text: At one hundred thousand connected vehicles, a one second stream becomes one hundred thousand decisions every second. VoltSight turns that telemetry into a live range risk and charging system. It tells fleet operators which electric vehicles are at risk, why they are at risk, and where they can charge. What you see is the real application, running on synthetic fleet data.

The problem. The range on the dashboard is not usable range. It depends on the vehicle, the route, temperature, load and battery age, and it changes the moment a charger fails. Charging at the wrong time is expensive, battery health is invisible, and at fleet scale an answer is only useful if it arrives in seconds. The official challenge asks for a hundred thousand vehicles and more than a hundred thousand events per second.

Here is the architecture. A Go simulator streams telemetry to a gateway over mutual T L S. Events land in Kafka, keyed by vehicle. A stream worker removes duplicates, tracks vehicle state, and runs the range risk engine, which looks up the distance to the nearest available charger from a graph overlay. Alerts return through Kafka to an alert service that writes to PostgreSQL and publishes to Redis. ClickHouse keeps the history. The A P I serves the React console with J S O N and server sent events, and Keycloak handles identity. The stores differ because the access patterns differ: PostgreSQL for transactions and tenant isolation, Redis for hot state, ClickHouse for analytics. On the same host, ClickHouse ingested about four times faster than PostgreSQL.

title: Live dashboard
text: This is the live dashboard. The tenant has forty thousand registered vehicles, and eight hundred are reporting live right now. The cards show vehicles moving or charging, average state of charge, critical and warning alerts, and the charger network. In this demo scenario the simulator starts some vehicles at low charge and, five minutes in, takes most chargers out of service, so alerts appear through the real pipeline, not inserted into the database.

title: Fleet map — risk concentration and city filters
text: The map shows the fleet. Markers and clusters come from the backend, coloured by risk: green is normal, orange is low range, red is critical, and blue are chargers. The city buttons fly to Chennai, Bengaluru or Surat and filter on the server. One honest note: the basemap tiles come from Open Free Map, which this recording environment could not reach, so the app shows its markers only fallback. On a normal connection the same map draws roads and labels.

title: Alert evidence and route to a reachable charger
text: Open an alert. This is the key operational decision. It shows the state of charge, the estimated range, the range left after a safety margin, the nearest available charger, and the route to it, computed with A star over the road graph. The decision itself is a constant time lookup into a shortest path overlay that updates incrementally when a charger fails.

title: Charge Ops Copilot — tools, tenant authorisation, citations
text: The Charge Ops Copilot answers from tools, not from memory. Ask which vehicles are at risk. It calls typed, allow listed tools. The tenant comes from the authenticated token, never from the model. Every answer cites alert identifiers or says insufficient evidence. Any write, such as a charging plan, is only proposed: a human approves it, and every step is audited. In this build the default provider is a deterministic stub, so no external language model produced this answer.

Under the interface, this is a distributed streaming platform. Prometheus scrapes the gateway and the worker. SQL tuning was measured with real query plans: a deep alert page fell from one point three seconds to a fraction of a millisecond with keyset pagination and a partial index. Security includes row level security, role based access, and an OWASP ZAP baseline with fifty eight checks passed, zero failures, and three documented warning groups.

Every requirement is traced to evidence, with honest statuses. Of sixty requirements, twenty eight pass, twenty eight are partial, two are blocked and two fail. Measured: ninety eight point three thousand events per second for sixty seconds with a hundred thousand vehicles; zero events lost in a three times burst and five chaos scenarios; A P I ninety fifth percentile latency of twenty seven milliseconds. The five second critical alert target was not met at that load on one host, and soak, scale out and production cloud deployment were not run.

title: VoltSight — EV Fleet Range-Risk & Charge Orchestration
text: VoltSight closes the loop from telemetry to decision: detect the risk, explain the evidence, find a reachable charger, and keep the operator in control. The architecture is designed to carry that workflow from this demonstration toward a production fleet platform. VoltSight, E V fleet range risk and charge orchestration. Code and documents are in the GitHub repository.
